title: Training Webpage Template - User Guide
text:
Welcome to the SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template User Guide!
When you give a training, participants need one place to find the schedule, the materials and the practical information. And once the training is over, others should be able to find, cite and reuse it. The SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template, made by the SciLifeLab Training Hub, gives you a website that does both. This guide shows you how to make it your own, step by step.

The template works for most kinds of training: online or in person, recurring or one-off, self-paced, or in cohorts. Want to look around? Visit the example training website.

What you get


Ready to use
A complete, SciLifeLab-branded website: overview, schedule, syllabus, team, information pages and room for your materials.


No programming
You fill in your information in text files, and write your materials in Markdown. The website is built and published for you.


FAIR by default
Your training gets a citation, a licence and information that registries can read, from the same text files.




Before you start
All you need is a computer and a free GitHub account. You don’t need any experience with Git, Python or Quarto: the guide explains every step.
The chapters follow the order in which you build your website: setting up your copy, the landing page, your training instances and materials, and finally making your training FAIR. Work through them in order the first time. Later, you can go straight to the chapter you need.
Start with: Set up your training →


Need help?
Contact the SciLifeLab Training Hub at training@scilifelab.se.

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.1 Install the software
To turn the SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template into a website for your own training, you first need your own copy of the template. This chapter takes you through everything you need to do once, at the start: you will create your own copy, publish it as a website, and set it up on your computer so you can edit it.
The figure below shows the steps you will follow:
Once you are done, the next chapter, Regular workflow, shows the steps you repeat every time you want to update your training website.
To work with the template, you need a free GitHub account and four free programs. If you already have some of them, you can skip those. Install each program with the default settings.

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.2 Create your repository
A repository is the folder on GitHub that holds everything for your training: the information about it, the materials, and the website. Follow these steps to create your own repository as a copy of the template:

Open the SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template on GitHub.
In the top-right corner of the page, click the green Use this template button and select Create a new repository.



Fill in the form:

Turn Include all branches on. This is required!
Under Owner, select the GitHub organisation or account where the repository should live, for example SciLifeLab-Training, NBISweden, or your personal account.
Under Repository name, enter a short name in lowercase, with hyphens instead of spaces, for example introduction-to-r. The name becomes part of your website URL, so choose it carefully.
Under Visibility, choose Public, so participants can see the website and materials.

Click Create repository.


GitHub now opens your new repository. Check the name at the top of the page: it should be the name you just chose, not the template’s name.







TipWorking with others? Add collaborators (optional)





If other people will help develop or maintain the training, give them access to the repository. You can also come back to this later.

In your repository, click Settings. 
Under Access in the menu on the left, click Collaborators and teams. 
Click Add people or Add teams.
Search for the person or team, choose a role, and click Add. 

The options you see depend on whether the repository belongs to you or to an organisation, and on your permissions in that organisation.

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.3 Publish your website
Your new repository contains a full copy of the template website. From the files in your repository, GitHub automatically builds your training website, and publishes it at its own web address.
In this step, you check two settings to make sure your website is online and can be updated, and you add the link to your website to the main page of your repository.

Check that your website is online

In your repository, click Settings, then Pages in the menu on the left. 
At the top of the page, look for Your site is live at, followed by your website address. It looks like https://ORGANISATION.github.io/REPOSITORY-NAME/, with your organisation (or user name) and repository name filled in. 







NoteDon’t see “Your site is live at”?





Sometimes GitHub doesn’t switch on publishing by itself. You can do it yourself:

On the same page, under Source, choose Deploy from a branch.
Under Branch, choose gh-pages and / (root), and click Save. 
Wait a minute or two and refresh the page. Your site is live at now appears at the top.






Check that your website can be updated
Every time you send a change to GitHub, GitHub runs a small automatic process that rebuilds your website. This process needs permission to update the website.

Click Settings, then Actions → General in the menu on the left.
Scroll down to Workflow permissions, and check that Read and write permissions is selected. 







NoteIs “Read repository contents and packages permissions” selected instead?





Select Read and write permissions and click Save.
If you can’t select it because the option is greyed out, your organisation controls this setting. Ask an administrator of the organisation to allow it for your repository.





Add the website link to your repository
Show the website address on your repository’s main page, so you can always find your website quickly:

Click the Code tab to go back to the repository’s main page. 
On the right-hand side, next to About, click the gear icon ⚙️.
Tick Use your GitHub Pages website and click Save changes.

title: 2  Set up your training
section: 2.4 Open the repository on your computer
text:
2.4 Open the repository on your computer
So far, your repository only exists on GitHub. To edit it, you make a copy of it on your computer. This is called cloning. Working on a copy has a big advantage: nothing you change is visible to anyone else until you decide to send it to GitHub. You can try things out, look at the result, and undo mistakes, all safely on your own computer.
You work on your copy in Visual Studio Code, or VS Code for short: a free program for editing text files. You will use it for most of your work: to open and edit your files, to see a preview of your website, and to send your changes to GitHub.
To clone your repository and open it in VS Code:

On your repository’s main page on GitHub, click the green Code button, make sure HTTPS is selected, and copy the address.

Open Visual Studio Code (VS Code) and click Clone Git Repository on the start screen. If you don’t see it, open View → Command Palette, type Git: Clone and press Enter.

Paste the HTTPS address you copied and press Enter.
Choose where to save the repository on your computer, for example a folder called GitHub inside Documents, and click Select as Repository Destination.

When VS Code asks whether to open the repository, click Open.

The files and folders of your repository now appear in the Explorer panel on the left side of VS Code. Throughout this guide, you open files by clicking them there.
If VS Code suggests installing recommended extensions, click Install. They help VS Code understand the files used in the template.







TipPrefer the terminal?





cd ~/Documents/GitHub
git clone https://github.com/ORGANISATION/REPOSITORY-NAME.git
Then open the new folder in VS Code with File → Open Folder…

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
2.5 Set up the environment
Your website is built by a few small Python scripts that come with the template. These scripts need one extra Python package. In this step you install it in a separate, self-contained environment inside your repository folder, so it doesn’t interfere with anything else on your computer.
You only do this once for each repository. You don’t need to understand the commands: copy each one exactly as shown.

Open a terminal
A terminal is a window where you type commands. In VS Code, choose Terminal → New Terminal.

The terminal opens at the bottom of the window, already inside your repository folder.
To run a command from this guide, copy it, paste it into the terminal, and press Enter.



Check the software
First, check that Git, Python and Quarto were installed correctly. Run these commands one by one:

macOS and LinuxWindows


git --version
python3 --version
quarto --version


git --version
python --version
quarto --version



Each command should print a version number, for example Python 3.12.4 (see image above). If one says command not found, install that program again, restart VS Code, and try again.


Create the environment
Run these three commands one by one. The last one can take a minute.

macOS and LinuxWindows


python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt


python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt



The first command creates the environment, the second switches it on, and the third installs what the scripts need. When the environment is switched on, the terminal line starts with (.venv):
(.venv) username@computer introduction-to-r %



Let VS Code switch on the environment
The environment has to be switched on each time you open a new terminal. You can let VS Code do that for you:

Press Cmd+Shift+P (macOS) or Ctrl+Shift+P (Windows and Linux).
Type Python: Select Interpreter and press Enter.
Choose the option that shows .venv.


From now on, every new terminal you open in this repository starts with the environment switched on.

title: 2  Set up your training
text:
You’re all set!
Your training has its own repository and website, and your computer is ready to edit it. You won’t need to repeat any of these steps for this training repository.
Continue with Regular workflow to make your first change and see it appear on your website.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.1 Open your training
Your training now has its own repository and website, and a copy on your computer that you can edit. This chapter shows you how to make edits in your repository. These are the steps you repeat every time you work on your training website: open your training repository in VS Code, preview it, make your changes, and publish them.
The figure below shows the steps you will follow:
The cheat sheet at the end of this chapter lists them all in one table.
Each time you start working, open your repository in VS Code and make sure you have the latest version.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
Open VS Code. It usually reopens the repository you worked on last. 
If not, choose File → Open Recent, or File → Open Folder… and select your repository folder.

Get the latest version. If you work together with others, they may have uploaded changes since you last worked. In the bottom-left corner of VS Code, click the circular arrows next to the branch name (Synchronize Changes). This downloads their changes to your computer.



Which part of your website are you working on?
Apart from having the latest version, you also need to make sure you’re working on the right part of your website. Your website has two kinds of parts, and your repository keeps each one on its own branch:

main branch: the landing page of your training.
release-xxxx branch: one training instance. Your copy of the template comes with one example training instance: release-0000.

The bottom-left corner of VS Code shows the branch you’re working on. Clicking it will open a list of all branches that your repository contains.

Branches are explained in more detail in Repository structure.
Before you start editing, always check that you’re on the branch you want to change. To move to another branch, see Switch branch.
For your first change below, stay on main.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.2 Preview your website
You’re now ready to start editing. Before you change anything, start a preview: it shows your website in your web browser while you work, and updates every time you save a file. That way, you see straight away what each change does.
The preview runs on your own computer, so only you can see it. Nothing is published until you decide to, so you can check every change before your collaborators or participants see it.
To start the preview, open a terminal (Terminal → New Terminal, see Open a terminal) and run:
python scripts/preview.py

Quarto now builds your website. After a few seconds, it automatically opens in your web browser.

If it doesn’t open by itself, copy the address shown in the terminal, for example http://localhost:4123/, and paste it into your browser.
Keep the preview running while you work. To see a change, save the file you edited: press Cmd+S (macOS) or Ctrl+S (Windows and Linux). The preview in your browser then updates by itself.
To stop the preview when you are done editing, click in the terminal and press Ctrl+C (macOS, Windows and Linux).






NoteWant to run another command while the preview is running?





The terminal running the preview is busy, so you can’t type other commands in it. Open a second terminal with Terminal → New Terminal, and run your command there.









TipAnother way to start the preview: the Preview button





When a page file (ending in .qmd) is open in VS Code, you can also click the Preview button in the top-right corner of the editor.

The website then opens inside VS Code. To see it in your browser instead, click Open in Browser.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.3 Make a change
With the preview running, you will now make your first change: adding the title of your training. You will then publish this change.
Almost everything on your website comes from the files in the data folder: the training title, dates, team, schedule, and so on. You change your website by changing these files, without touching any code. How these files are organised is explained in Repository structure.
To change the title of your training:

In the Explorer panel, open the data folder and click course.yml.

Scroll down a bit and find the line:
title: "Training title"
Change the text between the quotation marks to your training’s title, for example:
title: "Introduction to R"

Save the file with Cmd+S (macOS) or Ctrl+S (Windows and Linux).

The new title now appears at the top of the website preview in your browser.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.4 Commit and push your changes
Your new title now shows in the preview, but only on your computer: it isn’t on your public website yet. To publish it, you send your change to GitHub. This takes two steps, both in the Source Control panel of VS Code:

Commit: save a version of your changes, with a short description of what you changed. Each commit is kept, so you can always see what changed and when.
Push: upload your commits to GitHub. GitHub then updates your website automatically.

To commit and push your change:

Click the Source Control icon on the left side of VS Code. Your changed files are listed under Changes.







NoteMore files than you changed?



You changed only course.yml, but you probably see more files, for example in the _generated folder. That’s expected: while the preview runs, the template updates these files automatically from your data files. Depending on what you change, you may also see README.md, CITATION.cff or .zenodo.json.
Always commit all changed files together.


Hover over the word Changes and click the + next to it (Stage All Changes). This tells VS Code to include all changed files in your commit. They move to Staged Changes.

In the Message box at the top, describe your change, for example Change the training title.

Click Commit.
Click Sync Changes to push your commit to GitHub.








Note



The first time you push, VS Code may ask you to sign in to GitHub. Follow the instructions in your browser, then return to VS Code.








TipChanged something by mistake?





Before you commit, you can undo all changes to a file: in the Source Control panel, hover over the file and click the curved arrow (Discard Changes). The file goes back to how it was at your last commit.

You only need to do this for the files you changed yourself, such as data/course.yml. The files the template updates automatically, for example in the _generated folder, go back by themselves: as soon as you discard your own change, the preview rebuilds them, and they disappear from the list after a few seconds.
This only works while the preview is running. If they are still listed, start the preview (python scripts/preview.py) and wait a few seconds.

title: 3  Regular workflow
text:
3.5 Check the published website
After you push your local changes to GitHub to be published, GitHub rebuilds your training website by itself. This usually takes one or two minutes.
To follow it on GitHub:

Open your repository on GitHub and click the Actions tab.

Wait until both of these show a green checkmark:

deploy-landing (or deploy-instance, when you changed a training instance): builds your website;
pages build and deployment: publishes it.


A yellow dot means it is still running.
Open your website with the link under About on your repository’s main page, see Add the website link to your repository. Still seeing the old version? Wait a minute and refresh the page. Browsers sometimes show an older copy for a short while.

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
4.1 Branches
You now know how to make a change to your training website by changing data files in your training repository, and how to publish it. Before you replace all the template data with your training’s data and add your training materials, it helps to know how your repository is organised.
This chapter shows where each part of your website lives in the repository, so you always know where to make a change.
You will learn about:
Your training repository is divided into branches. Each branch holds the files for one part of your website. A new repository made from the template has three branches: main, release-0000 and gh-pages.
Each of these branches holds the files for one part of your website:
Because each training instance has its own branch, you can prepare the next training without changing the website of an earlier one. Participants of earlier trainings can always go back to the materials as they were.

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
The main branch holds the landing page: the general page about your training, with its description, learning outcomes and team, and links to every training instance.

The gh-pages branch holds the published website: the finished pages that visitors see. GitHub builds them from your other branches and updates this branch automatically every time you push a change.






Important



Never edit the gh-pages branch yourself. GitHub updates it automatically every time you push a change to one of the other branches.


The release-0000 branch is an example training instance: the website for one time the training is given, with its dates, schedule, practical information, team and training materials. You use it as the starting point for each new training instance, which gets a branch of its own.




Branch names
A training instance branch is named release- followed by the year and month of the training, written as YYMM. For example, release-2705 is the training instance given in May 2027. For self-paced training and training in cohorts, the year and month may mean something slightly different: see Training instances.


An example
This is what the branches look like in a repository for a training that has been given twice, in May 2026 and May 2027:
Your repository
│
├── main              The landing page: the general page about your
│                     training, with links to every training instance.
│
├── release-2605      The website of your training in May 2026.
├── release-2705      The website of your training in May 2027.
│
│
└── gh-pages          The published website. Updated automatically.
In this repository, you would work on these branches:



I want to…
I work on branch…




Change the landing page
main


Edit the materials of the May 2026 training
release-2605


Fix a typo on the May 2027 website
release-2705


Set up the next training instance
A new release- branch: see Training instances









Note



You work on one branch at a time. To learn how to switch to another branch in VS Code, see Switch branch.

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
4.2 Three kinds of files
When you open a branch of your repository in VS Code, you see many files and folders. Most of these you never have to edit, you only have to work with a few of them. On all branches, the files fall into three groups:








Icon
Kind
What it means for you




✏️
Files you edit
Your information and materials. This is where you make your changes.


🔄
Files that are updated automatically
The template creates and updates these files automatically. You should not edit them, but if you accidentally do, your edits will automatically be overwritten.


🔒

The parts that make the template work, you never need to change these.









Tip



The automatically updated files 🔄 often appear in the Source Control panel when you only edited one ✏️ file. That’s expected: commit them together with your own changes, as described in Commit and push your changes.

title: 4  Repository structure
text:
4.5 Data files
As the tables above show, most of the files you edit in the main branch as well as the instance branches are data files: the files ending in .yml in the data folder.

What you see in a data file
When you open a data file, for example data/course.yml on the main branch, you see three kinds of text. VS Code shows each in its own colour:


Explanations (grey in the screenshot): lines that start with #. They explain how the file works and what each field does, and don’t appear on your website. You can delete them if you prefer a shorter file, but they are useful to keep while you are getting to know the template.
Field names (green): the word before the colon, for example title:. They tell the template where each piece of information goes on your website. Never change field names. If you do, the template can’t find that information any more.
Values (blue): the text after the colon, usually between quotation marks. This is what you change. It is the information that appears on your website.

For example, in this line:
title: "Training title"
title is the field name: leave it as it is. "Training title" is the value: replace it with the title of your training.






Note



The colours depend on the colour theme you use in VS Code, so yours may look different from the screenshot. The rule is always the same: lines starting with # are explanations, the word before the colon is the field name, and the text after the colon is the value you change.




Three kinds of values
Values in data forms come in three forms:

A single line of text, between quotation marks:

title: "Introduction to R"

Several paragraphs, after |. Start each line with the same number of spaces, and separate paragraphs with an empty line:

description: |
  This training introduces R, a free and widely used programming
  language for data analysis.

  Through short demonstrations and hands-on exercises, you learn how to
  read, clean, summarise and plot your data.

A list: each line starting with - is one item. To add an item, copy a whole line, paste it below, and change the text. To remove an item, delete its whole line:

keywords:
  - "R"
  - "Data analysis"
  - "Data visualisation"


Keep the layout as it is






Important



Data files are very sensitive to layout:

Keep the number of spaces (indentation) at the start of each line exactly as they are. They show which information belongs together.
Keep the quotation marks around values.

If the preview shows an error after you save a data file, check these first. The error message usually names the file and the line.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
Before you start
You are now ready to make the template your own. In this chapter, we start with customizing the landing page, which is the front door of your training. It introduces the training as a whole, and helps visitors decide whether to register, or which training instance to open.
The figure below shows the parts of the landing page, and the names this guide uses for them.
In this chapter, you will learn how to:
How to create a training instance and add it to the landing page is explained in the next chapter, Training instances.
Everything in this chapter happens on the main branch, and almost all of it in three data files in the data folder:
Not sure how a data file works? See Data files.
Work as described in Regular workflow:
The cheat sheet at the end of this chapter sums up which file to open and what to change for each part of the landing page.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.1 Switch off template mode
Your repository starts as a copy of the template, so it still presents itself as the template, in two places:

the README.md file, the description shown on your repository’s main page on GitHub, which still describes the template instead of your training;
the yellow Want to use this template? banner at the top of the landing page (see the overview image above).

In this section, you replace the README and then switch off template mode, so your repository presents your own training.

Replace the README
The template comes with a ready-made README for your training, in docs/_template-README.md. Copy it over the current README, which describes the template:

In the Explorer panel, open the docs folder and then _template-README.md.

Select all text (Cmd+A or Ctrl+A) and copy it.
Open README.md in the main folder of your repository, select all text, and paste, so the copied text replaces it.

Delete the note at the top of the file, between <!-- and -->, and the line starting with > **Template:**.
Fill in the parts marked Write this yourself. The other parts, between <!-- generated:... --> lines, are filled in automatically from your data files.
Save the file.




Remove the template banner

Open data/website.yml.
Find the line:
template: true
Change it to:
template: false

Save the file with Cmd+S (macOS) or Ctrl+S (Windows and Linux).

This changes three things:

The yellow banner disappears from the landing page.
The generated parts of your new README now show your training’s details, from your data files.
CITATION.cff and .zenodo.json now describe your training instead of the template.








NoteOptional: delete the template files you no longer need





Now you have switched off template mode, two things on your main branch are not needed any more:

The docs/_template-README.md file
The entire _template folder

You can delete both: in the Explorer panel, right-click each and choose Delete.
NOTE: Keep the rest of the docs folder!
NOTE: Deleting these means you cannot switch template mode on again (by setting template: true), the preview will then stop with an error, because the _template folder is missing.









Tip



The README shows the details you have filled in so far. Did you not fill in the data files yet? No problem: the README updates by itself every time you change them.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.2 Customise the look
You can make the landing page your own by changing the organisation logos, the button texts and the banner image. All of these are in data/website.yml. Open it, and work through the parts below.

Logos
The logos in the hero show the organisations behind your training.
Add a logo

Save your logo on your computer as an SVG or PNG file.






Tip



Use a white version of your logo, or one made for a dark background, so it stands out against the dark teal of the hero.


Copy the logo file into the img/logos folder: drag it from your computer onto the folder in the Explorer panel in VS Code.

In data/website.yml, find the hero part:
hero:
   logos:
      - src: "img/logos/scilifelab-neg.png"
      alt: "SciLifeLab"
      height: 56
      primary: true
Add your logo below the existing one, with these lines:

src: where the file is: img/logos/ followed by the file name;
alt: the name of the organisation;
height (optional): the height of the logo in pixels, 56 if you leave it out.

For example:

Save the file, and check the preview. If the logos look like different sizes, adjust their height until they look about the same.


The logo with primary: true (SciLifeLab) is always shown on the right. Your other logos appear to its left, in the same order as in the list.
Remove a logo

In data/website.yml, delete all lines of the logo you want to remove, from - src: to its last line.

Save the file and check the preview, the logo should be gone from the landing page.
Optional: if you no longer need the logo file, delete it from the img/logos folder. In VS Code, right-click the file and choose Delete.



Button texts
You can change the text on the two hero buttons, and the heading of the All training instances banner:

In data/website.yml, find the labels part:
labels:
  hero_view_current_label: "Take me to the current instance"
  hero_registration_open_label: "Register now"
  instances_band_title: "All training instances"
Change the text between the quotation marks. For example:

Save the file, check the preview.


Note that this only changes the texts. Where the buttons lead, and when they are shown, is set in data/instances.yml: see Training instances.


Banner image
The All training instances banner shows a decorative image next to the buttons. You can replace it with an image that fits your training.

Copy your image into the img/images folder: drag it from your computer onto the folder in the Explorer panel in VS Code.







Tip



Use a landscape image. The image is cropped automatically to fill the space, so keep the important part near the middle.


In data/website.yml, find:
instances_band:
  image: "img/images/navet-band.png"
Replace navet-band.png with the file name of your image, for example:

Save the file, and check the preview at different widths of your browser window.


To show no image at all, change it to image: "".






TipIs the important part of your image cut off?





You can choose which part of the image stays visible. This is the only change in this guide in styles.css, the file that controls the look of the website, so make it carefully:

Open styles.css and search for .instances-band__image (Cmd+F or Ctrl+F).
In that block, find:
object-position: center;

Change center to the part you want to keep. For example, center top keeps the top of the image, and 30% center moves the visible part to the left.

title: 5  Landing page
text:
5.3 Describe your training
What the landing page says about your training comes from two data files: data/course.yml describes the training, and data/team.yml the people behind it. The information you enter in these files is also used in the README and the citation of your training, and helps people find it in Zenodo and training registries such as TeSS.
Both files contain explanations at the top and between the fields, in the lines starting with #. This section covers the main points; the explanations in the files give the details.

The training: course.yml
Open data/course.yml and work through the fields below, from top to bottom. You only change the values: the text after the colon. See Data files for how a data file is built and the different types of data values.






Important



Data files are very sensitive to layout:

Keep the number of spaces (indentation) at the start of each line exactly as they are. They show which information belongs together.
Keep the quotation marks around values.

If the preview shows an error after you save a data file, check these first. The error message usually names the file and the line.










Field
Where it appears
What to fill in




title
The hero, and the browser tab
The name of your training


subtitle
The hero, below the title
One sentence about the training (optional)


description
The Training content card
What the training covers, in a few paragraphs


learning_outcomes
The Learning outcomes card
What participants can do after the training


keywords
The Keywords card
Four or five short terms that describe the subject


topics
The Topics covered card
The main topics, as short phrases


language, target_audience, expertise_level, organizers, funding
Not on the landing page: in the README, the citation and the information for training registries
See the explanations in the file


licence, licence_url (under reuse)
The footer (“Licensed under …”), the README and the citation
CC BY 4.0 by default.



The other fields under reuse can stay empty for now:

doi, release_date and zenodo_communities belong to publishing your training on Zenodo, and are explained in FAIRification.
licence_id, website_url and preferred_citation can stay empty for most trainings. The template works out the address of your website, and creates the citation from your team, title and DOI.

For example, this is data/course.yml filled in for a made-up training, Introduction to R. The explanations starting with # are left out, so the whole file fits on one screen:

After saving the file, the preview shows the landing page with this information.







Tip




Subtitle: keep it to one sentence, and start it with an action verb such as Learn, Understand, Explore, Build or Apply.
Learning outcomes describe what participants will be able to do after the training. For guidance, see the SciLifeLab Training Hub resources on writing learning outcomes.
Optional fields: to leave out the subtitle, use subtitle: "". To leave out the funding, keep funding: [].
Licence: if you change it, also replace the text in LICENSE.md in the main folder of your repository with the full text of your new licence.





The team: team.yml
The Founders and Contributors cards at the bottom of the landing page list the people in data/team.yml. They are also credited in the README and the citation of your training.
Open data/team.yml and fill in each person. The comments at the top of the file explain every field. To add a person, copy a whole entry, from - given_names: to the line before the next person, paste it below, and change the values. To remove a person, delete their whole entry.






Important



Every person needs given_names, family_names, roles (Founder or Contributor) and affiliation. If one is missing, the preview shows an error that names the person and the missing field.








NoteRoles and authors



roles says what someone did: it is shown on the landing page and in the README. citation_author says whether they are an author of the training. Everyone is an author, unless you set citation_author: false. Only authors end up in the citation. On Zenodo, authors are listed as “creators”, and everyone else as “contributors”.


For example, this is data/team.yml for Introduction to R.

After saving the file, the Founders and Contributors cards on the landing page show the new team:

The team is also used for the citation of your training. Open CITATION.cff, .zenodo.json or README.mdin the main folder of your repository: the template has updated these from your data files, while the preview was running.

Note that ‘Jonas Ek’ had citation_author: set to false and is therefore not included in CITATION.cff.

title: 6  Training instances
text:
Before you start
Your landing page now introduces your training as a whole. The next step is to add the times your training is actually given, each with its own website and training materials. These are the training instances, which learners reach from the landing page.
In this chapter, you will learn how to:
How to switch off template mode and fill in the website of a training instance (its dates, schedule, team and materials) is explained in the next chapters, Instance pages - Data files and Instance pages - Content.
In this chapter, you work on two branches: the new release- branch, and main for the landing page.
Work as described in Regular workflow.

title: 6  Training instances
text:
6.1 What is a training instance?
A training instance is one time your training is given, for example in May 2027. Each training instance has its own branch in your repository, and its own website, with its own dates, schedule, team and materials. The landing page links to them in two places:

the current training instance, in the hero; 
all training instances, in the All training instances banner. 

Is your training self-paced, or given to several cohorts? The template works for those too: open the matching box below.






NoteSelf-paced training: what is a training instance?





In self-paced training, participants start whenever they like, so there is no “time the training is given”. Instead, think of a training instance as a version of your materials:

Create a new training instance when you update the materials substantially, for example a new module or a revised structure. Small fixes, such as typos, go into the current training instance.
Earlier versions stay online. Participants who started with an earlier version can finish with the materials they began with.










NoteTraining in cohorts: one training instance per cohort?





If your training runs in cohorts, groups of participants who follow the same training at different times, how you set up your training instances depends on how your training is organised: does each cohort need its own website, or do the cohorts share one?
Option 1: one training instance per cohort

When: each cohort has its own dates, schedule, team or announcements.
What it represents: one cohort, with its own website. Each new cohort starts from the previous one, as described in Create additional training instances.

Option 2: one training instance for several cohorts

When: the cohorts follow the same materials and website, and only their start dates differ.
What it represents: a version of your materials. List the cohorts and their dates on the website, for example in the announcements or practicalities (see Instance pages - Data files). Create a new training instance only when the materials change substantially.

title: 6  Training instances
section: 6.2 Create your first new training instance
text:
6.2 Create your first new training instance






ImportantAdding a training instance always takes two steps!




Create a branch for the training instance: this creates its website.
Add it to the landing page, in data/instances.yml on the main branch: this makes the website findable.




Choose a name
Each training instance branch is named release- followed by the year and month in which the training instance is given, written as YYMM (see Branches). For example:







Training instance
Branch name




May 2027
release-2705


November 2027
release-2711



The four digits also become the address of its website, for example https://ORGANISATION.github.io/REPOSITORY-NAME/2705/.
For self-paced training and training in cohorts (see What is a training instance?), use these year and month:








Your training
Year and month
Example




Self-paced
When the version is released
release-2705 for a version released in May 2027


One training instance per cohort
When the cohort starts
release-2702 for a cohort starting in February 2027, release-2709 for the next one in September


One training instance for several cohorts
When the materials are released
release-2702 for materials released in February 2027



Each branch name must be unique. So with one training instance per cohort, two cohorts can’t start in the same month.


Switch branch
Once you have chosen a name, you can begin creating your new training instance, on a new repository branch. A new branch is always created as a copy of an existing one, so you first have to switch to the branch you want to create a copy of.
For your first training instance: switch to release-0000, the example training instance that comes with the template.
To switch branch in VS Code:

Click the branch name in the bottom-left corner of VS Code.

In the list that opens at the top, click on the branch you want to switch to, here release-0000. Branches that are only on GitHub but not VS Code so far start with origin/: if you choose those they will be added on your computer.


The files in the Explorer panel change to the files of that branch, and the bottom-left corner shows its name.



Create the branch

Check that the bottom-left corner shows the branch you want to copy.
Click the branch name (release-0000), and choose Create new branch… in the list that opens at the top.

Type the name of the new branch, for example release-2706, and press Enter.

Open the Source Control panel and click Publish Branch. This puts the new branch on GitHub.

title: 6  Training instances
section: 6.3 Add an instance to the landing page
text:
6.3 Add an instance to the landing page
You’ve now created a branch, and with it the website of your new training instance. Visitors can’t find that website yet: the landing page doesn’t link to it. To add the landing page links, you edit data/instances.yml on the main branch. The landing page then links to your new training instance in two places:

the Take me to the current instance button in the hero;
the All training instances banner.

To add your first training instance to the landing page:

Make sure you’ve committed any changes you made on your new training instance branch, and switch to the main branch, as described in Switch branch.
Open data/instances.yml. It lists the training instances the landing page links to: one entry per training instance, from - slug: to sort_key:. The comments at the top of the file explain each field.

The list contains example training instances. Change the first one, with slug: "0000", into your own training instance: change its slug, label, instance_url and sort_key. If registration is open, add the link to the registration page or form under registration_url. Without registration, keep registration_url: "" and the registration button will disappear.
For example, for a June 2027 training instance with no registration:

Delete the other examples, 2505 and 2411: each whole entry, from - slug: to sort_key:. They are only there to show how the list works in the template, and link to websites that don’t exist in your repository.
Save the file, and check the preview: the hero button and the All training instances banner now show your training instance.

Commit and push your changes.

If you break one of the rules described in the file, the preview shows an error that explains what to fix.






TipOptional: delete the release-0000 branch





Once your own training instance exists, you no longer need the example release-0000 branch. You can keep it, to look up how something was set up in the template, or delete it:

Delete the branch: on your repository’s main page on GitHub, click Branches.

Click the bin icon next to release-0000.

Delete its website: on the gh-pages branch on GitHub, open the 0000 folder, click ⋯ at the top right, and choose Delete directory.


Only delete it when your own first training instance is ready. Your later training instances start from your own previous one, so you don’t need release-0000 for those. But once deleted, it’s gone!

title: 6  Training instances
text:
6.4 Create additional training instances
The next time your training is given, start from your previous training instance rather than from release-0000. That way, everything you prepared last time comes along: your materials, instructor notes, team and settings. The previous training instance keeps its own branch and website, so participants can always go back to the materials as they were.

Switch to your previous training instance branch, for example release-2706, and create a new branch from it, for example release-2711, as described in Create your first new training instance.
Update the information of the new training instance, such as its dates, schedule and team: see Instance pages - Data files.
Switch to the main branch, and open data/instances.yml.
Add the new training instance: copy the entry of the current one, paste it at the top of the list, and change slug, label, instance_url and sort_key. Add a registration URL if registration is open.
Make the new training instance the current one. In the entry of the previous training instance, change status: current to status: previous, and show_in_hero: true to show_in_hero: false.

Save the file, check the preview, and commit and push.







Note



The training instance with status: current is the one the ‘take me to the current instance’ hero button leads to. Every other instance in the list needs to have status: previous. For all instances that have status: previous, their websites automatically show a banner saying: This is an older instance of this training, with a link to the current one.








Important



If your previous training instance was published on Zenodo, empty version_doi and release_date under reuse in data/course.yml of the new branch: they belong to the previous training instance. See FAIRification.

title: 7  Instance pages - Data files
text:
Before you start
Now that you have created your training instance, it’s time to fill it with the information about your training. As on the landing page, you do this in several data files. For training instances, some of these data files are required: the website can’t be built until they are filled in. Others are optional: which ones you use is up to you, and depends on the type of training you give.
In this chapter, you will learn how to:
How to add your training materials and instructor notes to your training instance follows in the next chapter, Instance pages - Content.
Everything in this chapter happens on the branch of your training instance (for example release-2706), and almost all of it in the data files in the data folder.
Not sure how a data file works? See Data files.
Work as described in Regular workflow.
The cheat sheet at the end of this chapter sums up which file to open, and what to change, for each part of your training instance website.

title: 7  Instance pages - Data files
text:
7.1 Switch off template mode
Just like the landing page, your training instance branch still presents itself as the template, in two places: the README and the template banner. You switch off template mode the same way as on the landing page: replace the README, and then remove the template banner.






Note



Do this once, on the branch of your first training instance: the one you created from release-0000 (see Create your first new training instance). Later training instances start from your first training instance branch, so the changes you’ve made there come along: template mode is already switched off.



Replace the README

In the Explorer panel, open docs/_template-README.md, select all text, and copy it.

Open README.md in the main folder of your instance branch, select all text, and paste, so the copied text replaces it.
Delete the note at the top of the file, between <!-- and -->, and the line starting with > **Template:**.

Fill in the parts marked Write this yourself, as on the landing page (see the example). The other parts, between <!-- generated:... --> lines, are filled in automatically from your data files.
Save the file.







NoteOptional: delete docs/_template-README.md





You no longer need docs/_template-README.md. In the Explorer panel, right-click the file and choose Delete. Keep the rest of the docs folder.






Remove the template banner

Open data/website.yml.
Change template: true to template: false.

Save the file.
The yellow Want to use this template? banner disappears from the overview page, and all automatically generated files now describe your training instance’s details.

title: 7  Instance pages - Data files
section: 7.2 Fill in the required data files
text:
7.2 Fill in the required data files
Now you can make the website of your training instance your own. Every training instance requires three data files to be filled in: the website doesn’t built until the required information is present. If a required field is missing, the preview stops with an error that names the missing file and field.
The required data files are website.yml, course.yml and team.yml. This section goes through them one by one.

website.yml: the overview page
data/website.yml mainly sets what appears on the overview page, the first page of your training instance website. The figure below shows the parts of the overview page, and their names:

In data/website.yml, you set the logos, the welcome section, the registration banner and the texts of the quick links. The other parts of the overview page come from other data files.
The table below gives a general overview of what to change in data/website.yml to customize it for your training. More detailed explanations are in the file itself: the explanations in the lines starting with # give the rules for each field. Read them carefully as you work through the file.
Many of the changes work the same as on the landing page, so visit Customise the look for additional detailed info.








Part of website.yml
What it sets
What to do




navbar → logos
The logos in the navigation bar
Copy the logo file into the img folder, and add its details below the existing logo in logos with src, alt and height.


welcome
The title, text and image of the welcome section
Change title and text. For your own image, put it in the img folder, change src to its path, and describe it in alt


registration
The registration banner
Fill in opening_date, closing_date, the link under url and, if there is one, the fee under cost. Choose with after_closing whether the banner shows “closed” or disappears after registration closes. Without registration, set enabled: false


pages
The title, description and icon of each quick link
Change title, and description and pick an icon from Bootstrap Icons



For example, this is data/website.yml filled in for a made-up training, Introduction to R. The explanations starting with # are left out, so the whole file fits on one screen:

After saving the file, the preview shows the overview page with this information.

There are two additional fields in data/website.yml: footer and content. Leave them as they are for now. The boxes below explain what they are for.






NoteAbout the footer





You don’t need to change anything in the footer part of data/website.yml. The footer fills itself in:

The organisation (“By …”) comes from organizers in data/course.yml.
The licence (“Licensed under …”) comes from licence and licence_url under reuse in data/course.yml.
The GitHub logo links to your own repository, worked out automatically.

The built_with part credits the SciLifeLab Training Webpage Template, which your website is built with. Leave it as it is.









NoteAbout the content part





The content part at the bottom of data/website.yml lists the sections of your training materials, and the order in which they appear in the navigation. Leave it as it is for now: you’ll change it when you add your own materials, as described in Instance pages - Content.





course.yml: the training
data/course.yml describes your training instance, in the same way as on the landing page. The information appears on the overview page, the Syllabus page, the README and the citation of your training. It also helps people find your training on Zenodo and in training registries such as TeSS.
To add information about your training to data/course.yml, work through the file according to the table below. Some fields in data/course.yml are required - like on the landing page - and some are optional. Required fields are marked in the table below with *.
More detailed explanations are in the data/course.ymlfile itself: the explanations in the lines starting with # give the rules for each field. Read them carefully as you work through the file.






ImportantLeaving out optional fields



If an optional field doesn’t apply to your training, such as credits or examination, you can leave it out in two ways:

delete it: the field name and all lines that belong to it;
leave it empty: nothing after the colon, "" or [].











Field
Where it appears
What to fill in




title*, subtitle
The navigation bar, the welcome section, the Syllabus page and the browser tab
The name of your training, and one sentence about it


description*
The Syllabus page
What the training covers

The welcome section and the Syllabus page
The dates, as "YYYY-MM-DD"

The welcome section and the Syllabus page
How long, online or in person, how participants learn, and where


language*
The Syllabus page, the README and the citation
For example "English"

The Syllabus page
Who the training is for, and what they need to know or have before

The Syllabus page and the citation
What participants can do afterwards, and a few terms that describe the subject

The Syllabus page
Credits, and how participants are assessed, if at all

The Syllabus page and the footer; organizers also in the citation
The organisations behind the training

The Syllabus page
The address participants send questions to


reuse → licence*, licence_url

7.3 Fill in the optional data files
You have now added all required information your training instance needs to built its website. As you can see in your training instance branch, the data folder holds six more data files: data/schedule.yml, data/announcements.yml, data/practicalities.yml, data/preparation.yml, data/faq.yml, data/resources.yml. In these files, you can add more, non-required information about your training that might be useful for you and your training’s participants. The table below shows which information goes in which file, and where it appears on the website:








Data file
What it contains
Where it appears




data/schedule.yml
The schedule of your training: its sessions, breaks and other events
The Schedule page, with its own link in the navigation bar, and the Next up section on the overview page


data/announcements.yml
News and updates for participants
The Announcements page in the Information menu, and the two latest announcements on the overview page


data/practicalities.yml
The venue, travel, accommodation and food
The Practicalities page in the Information menu


data/preparation.yml
What participants need to do before the training, such as creating accounts or installing software
The Preparation page in the Information menu


data/faq.yml
Frequently asked questions, and their answers
The FAQ page in the Information menu


data/resources.yml
Further reading, useful links and tools for after the training
The Resources page in the Information menu



These data files are the flexible part of your training instance: you choose which ones you need, depending on what type of training you’re organizing. For example, a self-paced training has no schedule, an online training needs no practicalities about a venue, and a short workshop may not need announcements.

Fill in optional pages
To fill in the optional pages, first choose which files you need for your specific training instance using the table above.
For each file you need:
Open it, and work through the values. Read the explanations in the lines starting with # carefully. They describe what each field does, how the page behaves, and how to leave out one item or a whole section without breaking the page.






ImportantUsing a schedule? Read this first





The schedule needs a bit more care than the other optional pages. The website doesn’t just show your dates and times: it uses them to put the events in order, to show the date of each day, and to work out which event is next, for the Next up section and its countdown on the overview page. A mistake in a date or time can put events in the wrong order, or stop the website from building.

Each event, such as a lecture, an exercise or a break, is one entry, from - title: to content:. Every event needs a title, type, group, start and end.

Write dates and times exactly as explained in the file, for example 2027-05-12T09:00
Use one of the event types that are supported by the template: lecture, workshop, practical, discussion, break, welcome, lunch, presentation, assessment, group-work, exercise, consultation, quiz, feedback, seminar
Events with the same group are shown together, on their own tab of the Schedule page, in order of their start time. You can choose how you want to group events, for example:

By day, for a training over a few days in a row: "Day 1", "Day 2", "Day 3". The tab adds the date, for example Day 1 – Monday, May 17.
By week, for a training with one session a week: "Week 1", "Week 2".
By topic, when each topic is taught on its own day: for example "Getting started", "Data wrangling", "Plotting".
For example, events grouped under day 1:

delete the file, or delete everything in it.

While you are filling out or deleting the optional data files, the navigation bar and the quick links update by themselves. A page appears when its data file contains information. If the file is empty, or doesn’t exist, the page is left out of the navigation bar and the quick links.
Team and Syllabus are always in the Information menu: they come from the required files team.yml and course.yml.








Tip

title: 8  Instance pages - Content
text:
Before you start
Your training instance website now has its overview page, syllabus, team and other information pages, all built from data files. What’s still missing are the training materials: the pages participants work through. They are the heart of your training instance website.
The training materials work differently from the rest of the website. They aren’t built from data files: you write them yourself, as pages in Markdown, a simple way of formatting text. Each page with training material is a .qmd file in the content folder.
Next to your training materials, you can also write instructor notes, in the instructors folder. Where the training materials tell participants what to learn, the instructor notes tell instructors how to teach it. These are written in Markdown too.
In this chapter, you will learn how to:
Everything in this chapter happens on the branch of your training instance (for example release-2706).
Work as described in Regular workflow.
The cheat sheet at the end of this chapter sums up which file to open, and what to change, for each part of your training instance website.

title: 8  Instance pages - Content
section: 8.1 Organise your training sections and pages
text:
8.1 Organise your training sections and pages
Before you write your training materials, you first have to decide how to organise them. Most of your training materials are in the content folder of your training instance branch: the content pages of your website are built from there. In this section, you will learn how the content folder is organised, how to divide your materials into sections, how to add and remove sections, and how to make them appear on your training instance website.

Where your training material lives
You write your training materials in the content folder of your training instance branch. The content folder contains:

index.qmd: the Content introduction page, which introduces your materials and gives an overview of the sections. This file must keep the name index.qmd: the Content link in the navigation bar leads to it.
_metadata.yml: the settings for all pages in the content folder, such as the table of contents on the right. You don’t need to change this file.
One folder for each section, with one .qmd file for each page in that section.


As you can see, your training materials are divided into content sections. The template’s examples use modules: module-1, module-2 and module-3. But sections don’t have to be modules: you decide yourself how to organise your training materials. For example, a section can be a module, a day, a topic or a week. Choose what fits your training,
On the website, each section gets its own dropdown menu in the navigation bar of the content pages, listing the pages in that section: see the purple boxes and text in the image above.
For example, Introduction to R is a training of three days, with a few topics each day. Its content folder could look like this, with one section per day:
content/
├── _metadata.yml          Settings for the content pages: leave as it is
├── index.qmd              The Content introduction page: keep this name
├── day-1/                 A section, with its pages:
│   ├── introduction.qmd
│   ├── rstudio-basics.qmd
│   └── reading-data.qmd
├── day-2/
│   ├── tidy-data.qmd
│   └── filter-and-reshape.qmd
└── day-3/
    ├── introduction-to-ggplot2.qmd
    └── customise-your-plots.qmd


Add a content section
When you’ve decided how to organise your materials, you can start adding your content sections.






ImportantAdding a section always takes two steps




Create its folder in the content folder, with its pages.
List the folder in data/website.yml.

A folder that isn’t listed in data/website.yml doesn’t appear on the website.


Step 1: Create the folder and its pages

In the Explorer panel in VS Code, right-click the content folder, and choose New Folder….

Type the name of the folder, and press Enter. Use only lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens: no capital letters, and no spaces. For example: day-1, data-wrangling or module-4.

Right-click your new folder, and choose New File….

Type the name of the page, ending in .qmd, and press Enter. For example: introduction.qmd. Use lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens here too.
The new file opens. Type this header at the very top, with your own title, and save the file:
---
title: "Introduction"
order: 1
---

Add more pages to the folder in the same way, with order: 2, order: 3, and so on.

The pages appear in the section’s menu in the navigation bar, in the order of their order numbers. To change the order, change the numbers.
For example, these are the section folders and pages of Introduction to R:







Tip



Want to look up how to write something in Markdown? Keep the template’s example pages for now: don’t delete their folders, module-1 to module-3. In the next step, you’ll see how to keep them off your website, while they stay in your repository for you to look at.


Step 2: List the section in website.yml
Your new sections and pages are now in your repository, but they don’t appear on your website yet. To make them appear, list each section in data/website.yml:

Open data/website.yml, and scroll to the content part at the bottom. Each section has an entry of three lines, like this one from the template:

Copy a whole entry, from - id: to title:, and paste it below the last entry. Keep the spaces at the start of each line exactly as in the other entries.

Change the three values to your new section

id: the name of your folder, exactly as you typed it in step 1, for example day-1 for introduction to r.
label: the short name in the navigation bar, for example"Day 1".
title: the text visitors see when they hover over the section in the navigation bar, for example "Getting started".

The first time only: delete the entries of the template’s sections, module-1 to module-3, each from - id: to title:. This only removes them from your website. Their folders stay in the content folder, so you can still look at the example pages.

Save the file, and check the preview: your section appears in the navigation bar of the content pages.








Important



The id must be exactly the same as the name of the folder, letter for letter. If you rename a folder later, also change its id in data/website.yml, or the preview stops with an error that names the missing folder.


For example, this is the content part of data/website.yml for Introduction to R:

And this is how the sections appear on its website:



Remove a content section
You can remove a section in two ways:

Only from the website: the section disappears from the navigation bar, but its folder and pages stay in your repository. Useful if you might need the section again later, or want to keep it as an example.
Completely: the section disappears from the website, and its folder and pages are deleted from your repository.

To remove a section from the website only: in data/website.yml, delete the section’s whole entry, from - id: to title:, and save the file.
To remove a section completely, do these two steps, in this order:

In data/website.yml, delete the section’s whole entry. Save the file.
In the Explorer panel, right-click the section’s folder in the content folder, and choose Delete. This deletes all its pages too.







Important



Always delete the entry in data/website.yml first. If you delete the folder first, data/website.yml still lists a folder that no longer exists, and the preview stops with an error.

title: 8  Instance pages - Content
text:
8.2 Add content to your pages
With your sections and pages set up, it’s time to fill the content pages with your training materials. In this section, you work through the parts of a content page: the content part, where you write your materials, and the On this page list and Previous and Next links, which are made automatically. The image below shows the parts of a content page:


The content part
In the content part, you add the text, images, presentations, exercises and everything else of your training. You write it directly in the page’s .qmd file, below the header, in Markdown: a simple way of formatting text.
For help with Markdown, the template comes with its own guide: the example content pages. They show how to write headings, lists, tables, callout boxes, images, videos and links, each with the Markdown ready to copy and paste into your own pages.
Tips for adding images, PDFs and other files
To use images, PDFs, slides or data files on your pages, first put the files in the docs folder of your training instance branch:

Then link to them from your pages: the example page Images, presentations and videos shows how.

Only the files you link to from a page are published on your website. Files in docs that no page links to stay in your repository only.
Keep files small. GitHub warns about files over 50 MB, and large files make your repository slow to work with. For videos, an embedded online video, for example on YouTube, is usually the better choice.
Give every image a short description, for visitors who can’t see it. The example page shows how.

Tips for adding presentations
To share presentations on your training instance website, you have several options:







Option
Good to know




Upload files to the repository, for example PDF slides
Put the file in the docs folder, and link to it from your page: see Linking to a file or resource within your training repository. The file is kept in your repository, so it stays available as long as your repository does


Link to an online file, such as Google Slides
See Linking to resources hosted elsewhere. Easy to make and update together, but the link can stop working, or need access rights that others don’t have


Make presentations in Quarto
Part of your training website, and archived with it. More technical, and takes some getting used to



Example: a page of Introduction to R
This page of Introduction to R has headings, an image, a link to a file in the docs folder, an exercise with a hidden solution, and some R code:

And this is how it looks on the website:







Note



Code blocks are shown on the page, with a button to copy them, but they are not run when the website is built. Participants copy the code, and run it themselves.


Now write your own pages.
With the example content pages and the tips above, start with the Content introduction page, content/index.qmd: introduce your training materials, and give an overview of your sections, with a link to the first page of each. Keep the file name index.qmd. Then work through the rest of your sections and pages.


The “On this page” list
The On this page list on the right of each content page is made automatically from the headings of the page:

Headings starting with ## appear in the list. Use them for the main parts of a page.
Headings starting with ### don’t appear in the list. Use them for smaller parts within a main part.
Don’t use a heading starting with a single #: the page title, from the header at the top of the file, is already the main heading.



Previous and next links
At the bottom of each content page, Previous and Next links lead through all your materials in one sequence: first the Content introduction page, then the pages of each section, in the order of the sections in data/website.yml and the order numbers of the pages. The last page of a section links to the first page of the next one.
The links are made automatically, and show the title of the page they lead to. To change where they lead, change the order of the sections or pages, as described in Organise your training sections and pages.

title: 8  Instance pages - Content
text:
8.3 Write instructor notes
You have now added your training materials, which show participants what to learn. But your repository doesn’t yet say anything about how to teach those materials. That information is useful for everyone who teaches your training, and you can add it as instructor notes, in a separate folder: instructors.
In this section, you will learn why instructor notes are worth writing, what’s in the instructors folder, and how to write your own notes.

Why write instructor notes?
Instructor notes show instructors how to teach your training: for example, how long each part takes, what to prepare, and where participants usually get stuck. They are useful in different situations, for example:

Several people teach the training, for example taking turns, or each teaching a different section.
New instructors join, or the training is taught again a year later.
Others want to reuse your training. With instructor notes, they can teach it themselves without having to ask you. That makes your training much easier to reuse, which is one of the aims of FAIR training materials.



What’s in the instructors folder
The instructors folder mirrors your content folder: one file for each section of your materials, plus a README.md for the training as a whole. All files are written in plain Markdown.
For example, for Introduction to R:








File
What it covers




README.md
The training as a whole: who can teach it, the timing of each section, how to prepare, the technical setup, and what to do during and after the training


One file per section, named after its folder, for example day-1.md, module-1.md or data-wrangling.md
That section: its key points, teaching flow, materials, exercises, common problems, and what to skip if you’re short of time





Fill in the instructor notes
You are now ready to fill in the instuctor notes. For this, you don’t have to start from scratch. the template’s instructors folder comes with a skeleton to fill in, a README.md for the training as a whole, and module-1.md and module-2.md for its example sections. Use these files as a starting point: rename them, copy them, and fill them in. You’re also welcome to change the headings, or to write your notes in your own way: the skeleton is a suggestion, not a rule.






ImportantNot on the website, but not private either



Anyone can read your instructor notes on GitHub, and they are archived on Zenodo together with your materials.
Never write anything that must stay secret, such as passwords, access codes, or answers to exams and graded assignments. Once pushed, deleting it doesn’t remove it: it stays in the history of your repository.



Open instructors/README.md, and replace the example text with your own.
Rename module-1.md after your first section: right-click it in the Explorer panel, choose Rename…, type the new name, for example day-1.md, and press Enter. Then fill in the file.
For each other section, add an instructor file with the same name as the section’s folder. The easiest way is to copy a file:

In the Explorer panel, right-click an existing section file, for example day-1.md, and choose Copy.
Right-click the instructors folder, and choose Paste.
Right-click the copy, choose Rename…, type the new name, for example day-2.md, and press Enter.

Delete the template files you don’t use, such as module-2.md.
In the timing table in instructors/README.md, add a row for each section, with a link to its file.
Save your files, and commit and push them. Instructor notes don’t appear in the preview: to see how they look, open them on GitHub.

And these are the instructor notes for its first day, day-1.md:

title: 9  FAIRification
text:
Before you start
Your training website is set up, and your first training instance is ready. As a final step, the SciLifeLab Training Hub encourages you to make your training materials FAIR: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable. FAIR training materials are easy to find, can be opened by anyone, are described in a standard way, and can be reused and cited by others.
The template does most of this for you. All you need to do is fill in a few more fields in your data files. If you want, you can also publish your training on Zenodo.
In this chapter, you will learn:
You fill in the FAIR information on the branch of your training instance, for example release-2705, and on main. Publishing on Zenodo starts from the branch of your training instance. Each step says which branch to use: see Switch branch.

title: 9  FAIRification
text:
9.1 FAIR training: what and how?
The FAIR principles were first written for research data, but they apply just as well to training materials. You put a lot of work into your training. FAIR makes sure that work can be found, used and credited, also by people outside your own team, and long after the training has been given.
In practice, FAIR training materials are:

Findable: people looking for a training on your topic can find yours, for example in a search engine or a training registry.
Accessible: anyone can open the materials, without having to ask you for them.
Interoperable: the information about your training, such as its title, authors and licence, is written in standard formats. Other websites and tools can then read it automatically.
Reusable: others know what they’re allowed to do with your materials, how to credit you, and how to teach the training themselves.


How the template makes your training FAIR
Most of this is already taken care of: the template uses the information in your data files for FAIRification. The table shows what the template does for each part of FAIR, and what’s left for you to do:








FAIR
How the template does it
What you do




Findable
Keywords, and Bioschemas markup that registries such as ELIXIR TeSS can read
Fill in keywords


Accessible
A public website and repository
Nothing


Interoperable
Standard formats: CITATION.cff, .zenodo.json and Bioschemas
Nothing: the template creates them from your data files


Reusable
A licence, a citation with the authors and their ORCIDs, and instructor notes
Check the licence, add ORCIDs, and write instructor notes





The files the template creates for you
Websites and tools can’t read your training pages the way people do. To find and cite your training, they need the information in a fixed, standard format. The template writes that information for you, in a few extra files. You don’t need to open them, but it helps to know they exist.
Every time the website is built, the template creates or updates these files from data/course.yml, data/team.yml and data/website.yml:







File
What it’s for




CITATION.cff
How to cite your training. GitHub shows it as a Cite this repository button, and reference managers such as Zotero can read it


.zenodo.json
The title, authors, licence, keywords and funding, for Zenodo


The generated parts of README.md
The training information, contributors, citation and licence


Bioschemas markup, hidden in the landing page and the overview page
Lets training registries such as ELIXIR TeSS find your training.









Important



Never edit these files by hand: your changes are overwritten the next time the website is built. Change the data files instead.

title: 9  FAIRification
text:
9.2 Fill in the FAIR information
Most of this information is already part of your data files, so you probably filled it in already. Check these fields on the branch of your training instance, and on main:








Information
Where
Good to know




Licence
licence and licence_url under reuse in data/course.yml
Says how others may reuse your materials. The template uses CC BY 4.0. If you choose another licence, also replace the text in LICENSE.md


Authors
data/team.yml
Everyone in the team is an author in the citation and on Zenodo. To leave someone out, add citation_author: false to their entry: they are still shown on the website


ORCIDs
orcid for each person in data/team.yml
An ORCID is a personal identifier for researchers, so their work is always credited to the right person. Write it like "https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1825-0097"


Keywords
keywords in data/course.yml
Help people find your training on Zenodo and in training registries


Organisers and funding
organizers and funding in data/course.yml
Credit the organisations behind the training, and the grants that paid for it



Leave the other fields under reuse empty for now. You add the DOIs after publishing on Zenodo, and the rest is worked out automatically.






Tip



Ask everyone in the team for their ORCID before you publish on Zenodo. Zenodo copies the authors when you publish, so a missing ORCID can only be added later, by hand.
